problem: Scene graphs use fixed discrete relation labels (e.g. support, next-to) that drop information such as where an object sits, and they are static snapshots rather than being updated on the fly as an embodied agent explores.
motivation: Embodied agents need an expressive scene representation that is built online from egocentric views, tracks objects across views, and detects scene changes. Such a representation should support downstream tasks like room rearrangement without task-specific training.
key_idea: Learn continuous node and edge embeddings for objects and pairwise relationships with multi-view contrastive learning (MoCo/InfoNCE), aggregate them online via Hungarian matching, and link them to an embodied state graph for BFS planning and change detection.
insight: Contrastive multi-view consistency yields features that transfer: on linear probes CSR reaches 85.3 mean accuracy versus 84.3 for supervised [support] and 70.2 for supervised [sibling] baselines, and it gets 84.3 vs 69.3 on hard-negative retrieval. Replacing components with ground truth shows the rearrangement bottleneck is detection and matching, not exploration: GT-T is comparable to the full system, while GT-BT and GT-MBT give large gains. The YCB-Video tracking ablation shows that updating node features online is critical.
method: Local scene representation: Faster-RCNN (class labels discarded) gives n boxes; all n^2 ordered pairs plus the image go through a ResNet-18 encoder with 5-channel input (RGB + 2 box masks), giving n node and n^2-n edge features in R^512.

Contrastive learning: MoCo-style momentum encoder with InfoNCE (queue 1024, tau 0.07, momentum 0.999) pulls the same relationship seen from different views together, assuming a static scene within a trajectory.

Global aggregation M_CSR: cosine-similarity matrix between local and global nodes, Hungarian assignment, matches above 0.5 are averaged into existing nodes, and unmatched nodes/edges are added as new ones.
Embodied state graph: one state per egocentric observation, holding references to the CSR nodes seen there, with action transitions between states; BFS gives the action path to a target node.

Between-trajectory object features: a separate feature trained with positives from different scene initializations matches object instances across walkthrough and unshuffle (threshold 0.4). Objects whose scene node similarity falls below 0.8 are flagged as moved.
Exploration policy: 3 conv layers + GRU, trained with DD-PPO for 200M steps on a reward for new positions and new objects, with no rearrangement notion.
Rearrangement pipeline: fuse walkthrough and unshuffle state graphs at the initial state, find moved objects, and BFS-plan to pick up and place them.

setting.backbone: ResNet-18 CSR encoder (MoCo contrastive, trained from scratch) + Faster-RCNN (Detectron2) + 3-conv/GRU exploration policy (DD-PPO)
setting.training_data: ~900K object node/edge relations from AI2-THOR (80 train rooms x 20 poses x 5 initializations, ~600K train); Faster-RCNN on ~10k AI2-THOR + ~127k LVIS images; policy trained 200M steps in 80 rooms; no rearrangement-specific training
setting.simulator: AI2-THOR (RoomR rearrangement); YCB-Video real data for tracking
setting.privileged: none for the main system (GT boxes/matching/trajectories only in ablations; GT boxes in YCB-Video tracking; assumes the same start pose for both phases)

numbers.evidence: Table 1 Downstream Rearrangement, CSR (Ours) Test column

numbers_note: Tables in the paper report values as 100x Success; YCB-Video ARI results are only in a figure. No standard navigation benchmark is evaluated.
results: With no task-specific training, CSR gets 0.4 Success / 1.9 %FixedStrict on the RoomR test set, versus 0.2 / 0.7 for VRR and 0.3 / 1.4 for VRR+Map. Its %E of 1.17 is worse than the baselines' 1.12 and 1.10, and absolute rearrangement success remains very low. Oracle components raise test Success to 10.0.
limitations: Absolute rearrangement success is very low and %E is worse than the baselines; the pipeline is bottlenecked by detection and cosine-similarity matching.
Ignores object state (e.g. open/closed) and cannot rearrange such changes, and agent-object interactions do not update the representation.
Relies on the same start pose to fuse the two trajectories' state graphs and on simple BFS planning over a state graph.
